content: Children and adolescents who have experienced traumatic events are at a significantly increased risk of developing post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and other adverse emotional, behavioral, and mental health outcomes. These outcomes can lead to substantial personal and healthcare-related burdens. A variety of psychological interventions are employed to mitigate these negative effects and prevent the development of PTSD in this population. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of psychological therapies in preventing PTSD and associated adverse outcomes in children and adolescents who have been exposed to trauma. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including The Cochrane Library, EMBASE, MEDLINE, and PsycINFO, up to May 29, 2015. The search included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) without restrictions on language, publication date, or status. Reference lists of relevant studies and reviews were also examined. The review included RCTs that compared psychological therapies to control conditions such as treatment as usual, waiting lists, no treatment, pharmacological interventions, or other therapies. Data extraction was performed independently by two reviewers, and statistical analyses were conducted using a random-effects model. Outcomes were categorized as short-term (up to one month post-therapy), medium-term (one month to one year post-therapy), and long-term (one year or more post-therapy). A total of 51 trials involving 6,201 participants were included in the analysis. Among these, 20 studies focused exclusively on children, two on preschool-aged children, and ten on adolescents, while the remaining studies included both children and adolescents. Participants in these trials had been exposed to various types of trauma, including sexual abuse (12 trials), war or community violence (10 trials), physical trauma (6 trials), natural disasters (6 trials), interpersonal violence (3 trials), life-threatening illnesses (1 trial), and physical abuse or maltreatment (1 trial). Other trials included participants exposed to a range of traumatic events. The majority of trials compared psychological therapies to control conditions such as treatment as usual, waiting lists, or no treatment. Seventeen trials utilized cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT), four employed family therapy, three used debriefing, and two trials each involved eye movement desensitization and reprocessing (EMDR), narrative therapy, psychoeducation, and supportive therapy. One trial each provided exposure therapy and a combination of CBT with narrative therapy. Additionally, eight trials compared CBT to supportive therapy, two compared CBT to EMDR, and one trial each compared CBT to psychodynamic therapy, exposure therapy combined with supportive therapy to supportive therapy alone, and narrative therapy combined with CBT to CBT alone. Four trials compared individual delivery of psychological therapy to group-based delivery, and one trial compared CBT for children alone to CBT for both children and their mothers. The findings indicated that children and adolescents who received psychological therapy were significantly less likely to be diagnosed with PTSD within one month of treatment compared to those who received no treatment, treatment as usual, or were on a waiting list (odds ratio [OR] 0.51, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.34 to 0.77; number needed to treat for an additional beneficial outcome [NNTB] 6.25, 95% CI 3.70 to 16.67; five studies; 874 participants). However, the overall quality of evidence for this outcome was rated as very low. PTSD symptoms were also significantly reduced within one month of therapy (standardized mean difference [SMD] -0.42, 95% CI -0.61 to -0.24; 15 studies; 2,051 participants), but the quality of evidence for this outcome was rated as low. These beneficial effects of psychological therapies were not observed over the longer term. When comparing specific therapies, CBT was found to be neither more nor less effective than EMDR or supportive therapy in reducing PTSD diagnoses in the short term (OR 0.74, 95% CI 0.29 to 1.91; two studies; 160 participants). However, this evidence was of very low quality. For the reduction of PTSD symptoms in the short term, there was a small but statistically significant effect favoring CBT over EMDR, play therapy, and supportive therapies (SMD -0.24, 95% CI -0.42 to -0.05; seven studies; 466 participants). The quality of evidence for this outcome was rated as moderate. No studies were identified that directly compared pharmacological therapies to psychological therapies. In conclusion, the meta-analyses provide some evidence supporting the short-term effectiveness of psychological therapies in preventing PTSD and reducing symptoms in children and adolescents exposed to trauma. However, the confidence in these findings is limited due to the low quality of the included studies and significant variability between them. There is a pressing need for high-quality research to establish the relative effectiveness of different psychological therapies for this population, particularly over the long term.
